content: Cnicus benedictus, commonly known as Blessed Thistle, is the only species within the genus Cnicus. It is a thistle-like plant belonging to the family Asteraceae and is native to the Mediterranean region, specifically from Portugal in the west, extending north to southern France and eastward to Turkey. This plant is also sometimes referred to as Cursed Thistle. Blessed Thistle is an annual plant that can grow up to 60 cm in height. Its leaves are leathery and covered with fine hairs, measuring up to 30 cm in length and 8 cm in width. The leaf margins are adorned with small spines. The plant produces yellow flowers that are arranged in dense flower heads, or capitula, which are 3–4 cm in diameter. These flower heads are surrounded by numerous spiny basal bracts. Some botanists include the related genus Notobasis within Cnicus, although Notobasis is distinguished by its slender, more spiny leaves and purple flowers. Medical Uses Blessed Thistle has historically been used as an herbal remedy to promote lactation. It contains approximately 2% cnicin, a compound thought to contribute to its medicinal properties. Additionally, it has been a component in traditional bitters formulas, which were used to address digestive issues. Edibility Unlike other thistle species such as Cirsium, Arctium, and Onopordum, Blessed Thistle is not considered edible. Its leaves are generally regarded as unpalatable and are often described as bitter.
